scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows · D4 Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
scenarios.brief: A fintech runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions on a TypeScript and Go monorepo, about 180 pull requests a week. Three workloads: a pre-merge review that posts inline comments at file and line, test generation for uncovered branches, and a nightly technical-debt sweep over roughly 2,000 files. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed. Developer trust in the review is low after a run of noisy findings.

scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.domains: D4 Prompt Engineering & Structured Output · D5 Context & Reliability · D1 Agentic Architecture
scenarios.brief: A logistics company extracts vendor, invoice and PO numbers, line items, totals, currency and Incoterm from commercial invoices and bills of lading, then posts them to an ERP. About 15,000 documents a month arrive in some 40 vendor layouts, including OCR'd faxes. Extraction uses tool use with a JSON schema and a validation-and-retry loop before posting; clerks handle exceptions.

questions.question: The review step runs claude "Check this diff for injection risks and report findings", and a later step turns its stdout into inline comments. On every run the review step sits idle until GitHub's six-hour limit cancels it, after which the comment step fails with 'Unexpected end of JSON input'. The engineer who wrote the step tested it in a terminal, where it worked: they read the answer and typed /exit. The Actions runner provides no TTY. What should the review step run instead?

options.t: Add --output-format json plus a --json-schema for findings to the current command, and parse that.
options.why: Runner-up. Structured output is the right way to feed the comment step, and it would win if the step finished and its prose were hard to parse. Here nothing is produced at all because the session never ends; the JSON error is a downstream symptom.

options.t: Wrap the command in an expect script that allocates a pseudo-terminal and sends /exit once the answer has appeared.
options.why: Incorrect. It fakes the person at the keyboard instead of not needing one. It is brittle (it must guess when the answer is complete) and the supported mode already exists.

options.t: Run claude -p with the same prompt text, and have the next step read whatever it prints to standard output.
options.why: Correct. The CLI is waiting for a person to type the next turn, exactly as it did in the engineer's terminal. -p (--print) is non-interactive mode: it answers once, prints and exits.

options.t: Export CLAUDE_CODE_HEADLESS=1 in the step's environment, and leave the command and its prompt as they are.
options.why: Incorrect. No such variable switches Claude Code into non-interactive mode. The supported switch is the -p flag.

questions.decider: The step idles until cancelled and the author ended the session by hand with /exit, so the session is waiting for input; if the step finished but its prose were unparseable, structured output flags would be the fix.
questions.explanation: In CI, Claude Code must run in print mode (-p / --print): one prompt in, one answer out, then exit. Output format flags shape what comes out, but they do not stop an interactive session from waiting for its next turn.

eli5.question: The CI job never finishes, and the next step then complains about empty JSON. The clue is: the author tested it by reading the answer and typing /exit by hand. So the question is how to run Claude Code with nobody at the keyboard. It is not really about JSON.
eli5.answer: Think of a shop assistant who serves you and then waits for your next request until you say goodbye. In CI nobody says goodbye, so it waits for six hours. Print mode (-p) is the 'serve once and close the till' mode: it answers, prints, and exits. The JSON error only happened because nothing was printed. Rule: in a pipeline, run Claude Code with -p.
options: Runner-up. Asking for JSON (structured output) would help if the job finished and the text was hard to read. Here the job never finishes.
A robot that types /exit for you (expect) is a fragile workaround. A proper non-interactive mode already exists.
Correct. -p answers once and exits, which is what an unattended job needs.
This setting does not exist. The real switch is the -p flag.

deep.premise: It is tempting to read the JSON error as the problem and reach for output-format flags. But that error comes from the next step, after a six-hour cancellation. The review step itself never ended. An interactive Claude Code session waits for another turn until someone exits, and in CI nobody does.
deep.diagram:
claude "..."     -> answers, then waits for you (hang)
claude -p "..."  -> answers, prints, exits
  + --output-format json  -> same, but as JSON
  + --json-schema ...     -> JSON in your shape

questions.question: Inline comments are created by a Python script that runs regular expressions over the review's markdown to recover path, line and message. About 7% of comments attach to the wrong line, and 2% of runs post nothing because a heading or list style came back that the patterns never anticipated. Developers say the wording of the comments is fine. Nobody reads the review text directly; the script is its only consumer. Which change fixes this at the source?

options.t: Show two complete sample findings in the prompt, laid out in the exact heading and bullet style the patterns expect.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples are the best way to make a layout consistent, and they would win if a human read the review and wanted a stable format. A program still has to parse the prose, and the next unexpected shape breaks it again.

options.t: Pass --output-format json with a --json-schema naming path, line, severity and body, and read fields directly.
options.why: Correct. A program is the only consumer, so the review should hand it typed fields instead of prose to be re-parsed. The schema makes path and line values, not patterns to be guessed.

options.t: Review each changed file in its own invocation, so the job knows the path and only line and message need recovering.
options.why: Incorrect. Per-file passes help attention on large pull requests, but line and message are still pulled out of free text, and that is where both failures come from.

options.t: Feed the script's parse error back into a second run of the review whenever the patterns fail to match.
options.why: Incorrect. Retry with specific error feedback is a good loop for validated output, but here it pays for a second run to rescue prose that a schema would have made unnecessary. It does nothing for the 7% that parse but land on the wrong line.

questions.decider: The script is the only consumer of the review, so the output should be machine-readable fields; if people read the review and only the layout varied, few-shot examples of the format would be the better fix.
questions.explanation: When a program consumes model output, declare the shape: --output-format json with --json-schema turns findings into fields the posting script can read without guessing. Making prose more regular is still parsing prose.

eli5.question: A script tries to pick file names and line numbers out of written paragraphs, and sometimes gets them wrong. The clue is: no person reads the review; only the script does. So the question is what format a script should receive.
eli5.answer: Imagine posting a parcel by writing the address somewhere in a letter and hoping the sorter finds it. It works until someone writes the letter differently. A printed address label with fixed boxes (JSON output with a schema) is read the same way every time. Since only the script reads this review, give it the label. Rule: if a program reads the output, ask for JSON in a declared shape.
options: Runner-up. Showing examples (few-shot) makes the writing more regular. It would win if people read it. The script would still be guessing at text.
Correct. Fixed fields (path, line, body) that the script reads directly, with no guessing.
Splitting by file (per-file passes) helps attention. Line numbers would still be dug out of text.
Asking again after a failure (retry with feedback) costs a second run and does not fix wrong-line comments that parsed fine.

deep.premise: You might think the fix is to make the prose more predictable, since examples are the textbook tool for consistent format. That is the right tool when people read the output. When a program is the only reader, the real fix is to stop sending prose at all and send typed fields.

questions.question: The CI reviewer keeps asking for coverage on generated protobuf stubs, which the repository deliberately excludes, and keeps recommending the mock-factory fixtures the team replaced with builders last year. Developers see the same two suggestions when they ask Claude Code for tests on their laptops, and so does the nightly sweep. The conventions are written up in docs/testing.md, which the platform team edits through ordinary pull requests. Where should the fix go?

options.t: Pass the exclusions and fixture rules to the review job through --append-system-prompt in the workflow.
options.why: Runner-up. It would fix the CI review, and it would win if only that job were wrong. Laptops and the nightly sweep would still get the old advice, and a second copy of the rules would live in a workflow file nobody edits when conventions change.

options.t: Bake a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with both rules into the runner image all Actions jobs start from.
options.why: Incorrect. User-level memory in an image reaches CI jobs only, and it is not version-controlled with the repository. Developers' laptops are untouched.

options.t: Package both rules as a project skill in .claude/skills/ that the review prompt tells Claude to invoke.
options.why: Incorrect. Skills are on-demand workflows. Testing standards should apply to every session without anyone remembering to call them, including on laptops.

options.t: Add an @import line pointing at the existing standards document to the committed project CLAUDE.md.
options.why: Correct. Project CLAUDE.md is loaded by every Claude Code session in the repository: the CI review, the nightly sweep and each laptop. @import pulls in the existing document, so the conventions stay in one place that the platform team already maintains.

questions.decider: Laptop sessions and the nightly sweep show the same mistakes, so the conventions must load for every session in the repository; if only the CI review were wrong, a workflow-level system prompt would do.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is where a repository tells every Claude Code session its testing standards, fixtures and review criteria, in CI and on laptops alike. @import lets it reference an existing document instead of copying it.

eli5.question: Claude keeps suggesting things the team stopped doing. The clue is: the same wrong advice shows up on laptops and in the nightly job, not just the CI review. So the question is where to put the rules so every session sees them.
eli5.answer: Think of a staff noticeboard in the office kitchen versus a sticky note on one person's desk. The project CLAUDE.md is the noticeboard: every Claude session in the repository reads it. An @import line pins the existing testing document to that board. A note in one workflow only reaches one job. Rule: rules for everyone in the repo go in project CLAUDE.md.
options: Runner-up. A note added to one job's instructions (--append-system-prompt) would fix CI. It would win if only the CI review were wrong.
A personal settings file in the runner image (user-level CLAUDE.md) never reaches laptops and is not in the repo.
A skill is a recipe someone has to call. Standing rules should load by themselves.
Correct. Every session in the repo loads project CLAUDE.md, and @import reuses the existing document.

deep.premise: The stem opens on the CI reviewer, so it is natural to fix the CI job. But the same advice appears on laptops and in the nightly sweep. The fault is not one job's prompt; it is that no session in the repository knows the conventions.

workflow prompt    -> that one CI job
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md -> that one machine

questions.question: Over three months, human reviewers raised eleven problems in tests the pipeline generated, two of them asserting on the wrong branch; the automated review flagged none. To save a runner start-up, one invocation does both jobs: its prompt asks Claude to write tests for uncovered branches, then to review the whole pull request, new tests included. The review prompt lists general quality checks but says nothing specific about assertions. What change would most improve the review of generated tests?

options.t: Run the review as a fresh invocation that receives the diff, generated tests included, but none of the generation turns.
options.why: Correct. The reviewing session already holds the reasoning that produced the tests, so it reads its own choices as settled. A separate instance with no generation history checks them the way the human reviewers did.

options.t: Split the review into per-file passes followed by an integration pass over the changed and generated files together.
options.why: Incorrect. Multi-pass review fixes attention dilution on large diffs. The problem here is not breadth but that the reviewer wrote the code it is checking.

options.t: Add review criteria for generated tests: each assertion must target the branch the test names, with a failing sample.
options.why: Runner-up. Explicit criteria improve any reviewer, and this would win if the review already ran in its own session and simply lacked an assertion check. In the same session, the model still reviews tests it has just decided were right.

options.t: Enable extended thinking for the review half of the session, with a budget large enough to re-derive each test's intent.
options.why: Incorrect. More reasoning in the same context still starts from the generation reasoning. Independent instances catch more than self-review with extended thinking.

questions.decider: Generation and review share one session, so the reviewer carries the reasoning behind every test; if the review already ran independently, adding assertion criteria would be the better fix.
questions.explanation: A session is a weak reviewer of its own output, because its context still holds the reasoning that produced it. An independent instance with no generation history catches subtle issues that self-review, even with extended thinking, misses.

eli5.question: The automatic review never finds problems in tests the pipeline wrote, but people do. The clue is: the same run writes the tests and then reviews them. So the question is whether the reviewer can be fair to its own work.
eli5.answer: Think of proof-reading your own essay straight after writing it. You read what you meant, not what you wrote. A friend who has never seen it catches the slip. A fresh, independent instance is that friend: it sees the tests without the reasons that produced them. Rule: never let the session that wrote the code be its only reviewer.
options: Correct. A new session sees only the diff, like a friend reading your essay cold.
Reviewing file by file (multi-pass) helps with big diffs. The problem here is who is reviewing, not how much.
Runner-up. A checklist for assertions (explicit criteria) helps any reviewer. It would win if the reviewer were already separate.
Thinking harder (extended thinking) in the same session still starts from the author's own reasoning.

deep.premise: The two wrong-branch assertions make it look like a missing criterion: the prompt says nothing about assertions. But the reviewer never flagged any of eleven problems in generated tests. That pattern says the reviewer is the author, and an author re-reads its own choices as correct.
deep.diagram:
one session:  write tests -> review (sees own reasoning)
two sessions: write tests | review (sees only the diff)

questions.question: Developers sampled 300 review findings and judged 22% worth acting on. The biggest group, about a third of all findings, says a doc comment is stale; reviewers say most of those comments are fine. That group traces to one prompt line asking Claude to keep code documentation trustworthy. Since the spike, developers skim past the whole review, including its accurate security notes. What most improves precision?

options.t: Add three worked findings showing stale doc comments that merit a report, each with its file, line and suggested fix.
options.why: Runner-up. Examples are the best tool for consistent output, and they would win if the category were already defined as a checkable condition and only the findings' shape varied. Examples built on a vague goal still leave the boundary undefined.

options.t: Have a second instance grade every finding from one to five, and post only the findings it scores four or higher.
options.why: Incorrect. A grader judges against the same undefined idea of 'trustworthy' and doubles the cost of every review. Define the category first.

options.t: Rewrite that line as a test: report a doc comment only when the behaviour it describes differs from what the code does.
options.why: Correct. 'Trustworthy' has no boundary, so almost any comment can be flagged. A condition that compares claim and code can be checked, and categorical criteria are what move precision.

options.t: Tell the reviewer to stay conservative and to post a finding only when it is highly confident the problem is real.
options.why: Incorrect. Hedging words do not improve precision the way categorical criteria do; the model can be confident about a wrong stale-comment flag.

questions.decider: The noisy group comes from a prompt line with no checkable boundary ('keep documentation trustworthy'); if the category were already a concrete condition and only output varied, few-shot examples would be the better lever.
questions.explanation: Vague instructions produce vague findings. Replace a goal like 'trustworthy' with a condition that can be checked against the code, because a high-false-positive category erodes trust in the accurate findings too.

eli5.question: A third of the review's comments are wrong, and they all come from one line in the prompt. The clue is: that line asks for documentation to be 'trustworthy', which is a feeling, not a test. So the question is how to make that line precise.
eli5.answer: Imagine telling a referee to blow the whistle 'when play is unfair'. They will blow it all the time. Tell them 'when a player is offside', a rule they can check, and the whistles become right. The fix is a checkable condition: flag a comment only when what it says the code does is not what the code does. Rule: replace adjectives with conditions you can check.
options: Runner-up. Showing examples (few-shot) makes output consistent. It would win if the rule itself were already clear.
A second judge (grading pass) uses the same vague idea and doubles the cost.
Correct. A clear test (comment says X, code does Y) replaces a vague goal.
Saying 'be careful' or 'only when sure' does not tell the model where the line is.

deep.premise: Examples feel like the strongest prompt tool, and for consistency they are. But this is a precision problem: the category itself has no boundary. 'Trustworthy documentation' can be read as almost anything, so the fix is to define the category as a test first.

questions.question: The same kind of finding, a possible null dereference on a path that a caller guards, was posted as critical on one pull request and minor on another in the same week. Each severity level in the prompt is defined by a test the reviewer can apply, such as 'reachable from an unauthenticated request'. Most findings land at the same level on every run; the swings cluster on findings where two of the tests seem to apply at once. What most improves consistency?

options.t: Ask for a confidence value beside each severity, and lower a finding by one level when its confidence is below 0.7.
options.why: Incorrect. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so this replaces one unstable judgement with another.

options.t: Add three worked findings near the boundary, each with the code, the level chosen and a line on why the other level lost.
options.why: Correct. The written tests are fine; the inconsistency lives where two of them overlap. Few-shot examples that show the reasoning on borderline cases are the most effective way to make those calls consistent.

options.t: Expand each level's definition with extra qualifying conditions for guarded and partially guarded code paths.
options.why: Runner-up. Sharper criteria would win if the levels were vague. Here they are already concrete tests, and more prose adds more conditions to weigh differently at the boundary.

options.t: Run the review three times per pull request and post each finding at the severity that at least two runs assigned.
options.why: Incorrect. It triples cost on a blocking path and can still split on a boundary case. Voting hides inconsistency instead of teaching the boundary.

questions.decider: Each level is already defined by a checkable test and the swings only occur where two tests overlap; if the levels were vague prose, sharper definitions would come first.
questions.explanation: When instructions are already explicit but output still varies on borderline cases, few-shot examples are the most effective fix. Choose examples at the boundary and show why one level was chosen over the other.

eli5.question: The same kind of bug gets called 'critical' one day and 'minor' the next. The clue is: the levels are already defined by clear tests, and the wobble only happens when two tests both seem to fit. So the question is how to teach the tie-break.
eli5.answer: Think of a new judge at a baking contest. The rulebook is clear, but some cakes sit right between two grades. What helps is watching a few past borderline cakes being graded, with the reason. That is few-shot examples for the boundary. Rule: if the rules are clear but answers still wobble, show worked examples of the hard cases.
options: A self-reported score (confidence) is not reliable, so it just moves the wobble.
Correct. Worked borderline cases show how to break the tie, with the reason.
Runner-up. Tighter definitions (explicit criteria) would win if the levels were vague. They already are clear tests.
Voting across three runs costs three times as much and still splits on close cases.

deep.premise: Inconsistency feels like a definition problem, so the instinct is to write more careful rules. But these rules are already concrete tests. The swings happen only where two tests overlap. More prose cannot settle a tie; showing a few worked ties can.

guide.obj: 4.2 Few-shot prompting for consistency and quality
guide.quote: Few-shot is the most effective technique for consistent, actionable output when instructions alone are inconsistent.

questions.question: Finance wants the 50% Message Batches discount applied wherever it fits. Spend splits three ways: the nightly debt sweep, started at 22:00 and read at stand-up; a weekly dependency audit published on Mondays; and the pre-merge review, which costs the most. Branch protection makes the review's status check required before the merge button enables, and developers usually wait for it. None of the three uses a multi-turn tool loop. Which plan should the team adopt?

options.t: Submit only the weekly audit as a batch, and keep the sweep and the review on synchronous requests.
options.why: Incorrect. Overnight work read the next morning is the textbook batch case; keeping it synchronous gives up a saving that fits.

options.t: Submit the sweep and the audit as batches, and keep the review on synchronous requests.
options.why: Correct. The sweep and audit are latency-tolerant, so they take the discount. The review gates the merge button and someone is waiting, so it needs a response time that batches do not promise.

options.t: Submit all three as batches, and have the review job poll for its result before posting its status.
options.why: Runner-up. It would capture the largest saving, and it would win if the review were advisory rather than a required check. Batches can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so polling just holds the merge.

options.t: Submit all three as batches, and fall back to a synchronous call when a review result is late.
options.why: Incorrect. For the blocking review the fallback would fire on most runs, so the team pays for both paths and maintains two code paths.

questions.decider: The review's status check is required before merging and developers wait on it, so it cannot use an interface with no latency guarantee; if the review were advisory, batching it too would be best.
questions.explanation: Match the interface to who is waiting. Message Batches cut cost by 50% but can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so they suit overnight and weekly work, not checks that block a merge.

eli5.question: Finance wants the cheap slow option for everything. The clue is: the review is a required check, and developers sit waiting for it before they can merge. So the question is which jobs can wait for a slow, cheap answer.
eli5.answer: Think of choosing between economy post (half price, arrives within a day) and a courier (arrives now). Night-time reports and weekly reports can go economy. The review is a parcel someone is standing at the door waiting for. Use the Message Batches API only for work nobody is waiting on. Rule: batch it only if nobody is blocked waiting.
options: Too cautious. A report read the next morning is exactly what batch is for.
Correct. The two reports can wait for cheap post; the waited-for review goes by courier.
Runner-up. Batching everything saves the most. It would win if the review were just advice, not a required check.
A backup courier for a late parcel means paying twice almost every time.

options.why: Correct. A batch request cannot run a tool loop: there is no way to return the tool result and continue. The blame data is known in advance, so supplying it up front keeps the sweep on the cheaper interface.

questions.question: After the criteria rewrite, a reviewer labelled 400 recent findings and overall precision came out at 94%. The platform team now proposes letting findings block merges. Only that single overall figure was computed. Most of the 400 are null-safety or unhandled-promise findings; concurrency and floating-point findings, rarer but the ones tied to last year's production incidents, appear a handful of times each. What is the best next step?

options.t: Let only null-safety and unhandled-promise findings block for now, since they dominate the sample that scored well.
options.why: Runner-up. Gating only on well-measured categories is sound, and it would win if precision had been computed for each of those two. Only an overall figure exists, so neither category's own precision is known yet.

options.t: Let a finding block only when two independent review instances both report it, and post the rest as advisory.
options.why: Incorrect. Independent instances are good for review quality, but agreement measures repeatability, not correctness, and doubles the cost of a blocking check.

options.t: Label a new sample with a quota per finding category, and let each category block merges once its own precision clears the bar.
options.why: Correct. 94% is an average dominated by two common categories. A sample with a quota per category measures each one, including the rare categories that matter most, before any of them can block.

options.t: Let only findings the reviewer marks as high confidence block merges, and post the rest as advisory comments.
options.why: Incorrect. Self-reported confidence is an unreliable, uncalibrated proxy. It replaces measurement with the model's own opinion.

questions.decider: Only a single overall figure was computed, so no category's own precision is known; if per-category figures existed for the two common categories, gating on just those would be reasonable.
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can hide weak performance in specific categories. Measure each category with stratified sampling before letting it drive an automatic decision such as blocking a merge.

You need to check each group separately (stratified sampling). Then you trust each kind of finding only once its own score is good. Rule: an average can hide a weak group; measure each group before automating.
options: Runner-up. Blocking only on the two common kinds sounds safe. It would win if each had its own measured score; only the overall number exists.
Two reviewers agreeing shows they agree, not that they are right.
Correct. Sample each category on purpose, and let a category block only once its own score is proven.
The model's own 'I'm sure' (self-reported confidence) is not a measurement.

On those documents the model returns plausible values, sometimes the invoice number reformatted, sometimes the vendor code joined to the date. They pass validation and post to the ERP, where accounts-payable clerks later find them matched against the wrong orders. What is the right fix?

options.why: Runner-up. Checking against the system of record is good practice, and it would win if POs were printed but sometimes misread. Here the value never existed, so the lookup only catches some inventions, and an invented value that matches a real order slips through.

questions.question: Field accuracy is 96% on the six largest vendors and 71% on the thirty-four in the long tail. All eight worked documents in the prompt come from the big six, chosen because they were to hand. Tail layouts differ: totals printed above the items, tables running across pages, two vendors labelling the invoice number 'Ref'. Procurement signs roughly one new vendor a month, and their first invoices arrive before anyone has seen the layout. What most improves tail accuracy?

options.t: Swap most of the eight for tail documents with unusual layouts, each with a note on how its fields were located.
options.why: Correct. Examples teach generalisation when they show varied and ambiguous structures with the reasoning. Eight variations of formats already at 96% teach nothing new; varied tail layouts carry over to unseen vendors.

options.t: Add written layout rules: totals may sit above or below items, tables may span pages, and 'Ref' can mean invoice number.
options.why: Incorrect. Explicit rules cover the variations already seen. They do not show how to reason about a new layout, which is where few-shot examples beat instructions.

options.t: Keep a prompt per vendor with that vendor's own samples, chosen by the sender's address when a document arrives.
options.why: Runner-up. Per-vendor prompts would lift accuracy on known vendors and could win if the vendor list were fixed. A new vendor arrives most months before anyone has seen the layout, so there is no prompt for it, and forty prompts to maintain.

options.t: Extend the prompt to around forty samples, one from every current vendor, ordered from highest to lowest volume.
options.why: Incorrect. It adds a large token cost to every document and teaches recall of known layouts, not generalisation to the next vendor.

questions.decider: New vendors arrive monthly and their first invoices come before anyone has seen the layout, so the prompt must generalise; if the vendor set were fixed, per-vendor prompts would be a strong option.
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples should show ambiguous and varied structures so the model can generalise to new patterns. Choose them from where the model fails, not where it already succeeds.

eli5.question: The model is great on big vendors and weak on small ones. The clue is: a new vendor arrives about every month, and nobody sees their layout first. So the fix must help with layouts nobody has seen yet.
eli5.answer: Think of training a new post-room worker. Showing them eight parcels from the same courier teaches little. Showing a handful of oddly labelled parcels, and how you found the address on each, prepares them for parcels they have never seen. That is choosing varied few-shot examples. Rule: pick examples from the hard, varied cases, with the reasoning shown.
options: Correct. Varied tail examples with the 'how I found it' note help with new layouts too.
A written list of known quirks (explicit rules) does not prepare for the next new quirk.
Runner-up. A prompt per vendor (per-vendor prompts) would win if no new vendors ever arrived.
Forty examples cost a lot of space on every document and still only cover known vendors.

deep.premise: With 34 weak vendors, it feels thorough to give each vendor its own prompt. That works for vendors you already know. But a new vendor arrives most months, unseen. The prompt has to generalise, and that is what varied examples with reasoning do.

questions.question: On a labelled set of 200 recent documents, field-level accuracy is 97%, and the team wants to post to the ERP without review. The set was drawn at random from last month's intake, so OCR'd faxes, about 8% of volume, supplied sixteen of the 200. Vendor name is almost never wrong; multi-line item tables are where most of the errors sat. What should happen before review is removed?

options.t: Keep a random 3% of posted documents under clerk review each week, and stop review once a quarter passes cleanly.
options.why: Incorrect. Ongoing sampling is useful, but a random 3% has the same blind spot (few faxes), and it checks after posting rather than deciding what may post.

options.t: Calibrate a per-field confidence score on the 200 labelled documents, and route fields below the threshold to a clerk.
options.why: Runner-up. Field-level confidence calibrated on labelled data is the right routing tool once the labelled set represents each document type. Sixteen faxes are too few to calibrate faxes at all, so the threshold would be set mostly by clean PDFs.

options.t: Label a new sample with a fixed quota per document type, and report accuracy for every type and field pair.
options.why: Correct. A random sample barely covers faxes and averages easy fields with hard ones. A sample with a quota per type gives each type and field its own figure, which is what decides what can skip review.

options.t: Send line-item tables to a second, independent extraction instance, and post only rows on which both instances agree.
options.why: Incorrect. Agreement measures repeatability, not accuracy, and it ignores the fax problem. It is a change to extraction, not a measurement of it.

questions.decider: Faxes supplied only sixteen of the 200 labelled documents, so nothing reliable is known about them; with a labelled set that covered each type well, calibrating field-level confidence on it would be the next step.
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on specific document types and fields. Validate by type and field, using stratified sampling so rare types are measured, before automating; calibrated confidence comes after.

eli5.question: The team wants to stop human checks because accuracy is 97%. The clue is: only sixteen of the 200 checked documents were faxes. So the 97% says almost nothing about faxes.
eli5.answer: Think of tasting a soup from the top only. It tastes fine, but the bottom of the pot might be burnt. Before serving without checking, taste every layer (stratified sampling by document type) and judge each field on its own. Rule: measure each type and field separately before you automate.
options: Random spot checks after posting have the same blind spot and come too late.
Runner-up. A tuned confidence score (calibrated confidence) is the right router, but only once the labelled set covers faxes properly.
Correct. Sample every document type on purpose and score each type-and-field pair.
Two extractors agreeing shows they agree, not that they are right.

deep.premise: Calibrating confidence on labelled data sounds like the advanced, correct answer, and it is part of the end state. But calibration is only as good as the labelled set, and this set has 16 faxes. The first job is to measure each type and field properly; routing comes after.

questions.question: Scanned bills of lading reach the model through an OCR tool that returns over forty fields per text block, including per-character bounding boxes and confidences. A twelve-page document fills most of the context window this way, though extraction reads only each block's text and page number. The misses are line-item rows, dozens per page, and they cluster on pages four to nine, while the first and last pages come through cleanly. Which TWO changes together best address this?

options.t: Switch to a model with a larger context window, so the full OCR output sits well inside the limit.
options.why: Incorrect. The output already fits. A bigger window makes the middle bigger; it does not change how the middle is processed.

options.t: Reduce each OCR result to its words and page index before the tool result goes back to the model.
options.why: Correct. Tool results pile up and use tokens far out of proportion to their value. Two fields out of forty are needed, so trimming the rest shrinks the context sharply and loses nothing.

options.t: Open the document with a summary of its key fields and mark each page with an explicit page heading.
options.why: Runner-up. Key summaries at the start and clear section headings are a real mitigation, and would win if a few key facts had to survive. The misses here are dozens of rows per middle page, which no opening summary can carry.

options.t: Instruct the model to give middle pages the same attention as the first and last pages of the document.
options.why: Incorrect. Asking for attention does not change how attention is distributed over a long input.

options.t: Extract rows in passes of a few pages each, then merge the row lists from each pass in a final step.
options.why: Correct. Misses in the middle of a long input are the 'lost in the middle' effect. Short passes put every page near the start or end of some input, and the rows are exactly the detail that must survive.

questions.decider: The misses are dozens of line-item rows per middle page, too much detail for an opening summary to carry, so the input must be shortened and split; if only a few key facts had to survive, a summary up front with section headings would be the second change.
questions.explanation: Two forces are at work: verbose tool results filling the window, and the middle of a long input being processed less reliably than its ends. Trim tool results to the fields used, and split the work so detailed content never sits deep in the middle.

eli5.question: The model misses table rows in the middle of long scanned documents. The clue is: the misses are dozens of rows per page, and the OCR tool sends forty fields when only two are used. So the question is how to make the input smaller and stop the middle being skipped.
eli5.answer: Think of reading a 12-chapter book where every word comes with a page of notes about its ink and position. You would skim the middle. First, throw away the notes you never use (trim tool output). Then read a few chapters at a time and combine your lists (split into passes), so no chapter is ever deep in the middle. Rule: trim what you don't use, and keep important detail away from the middle of a long input.
options: A bigger window just makes a bigger middle.
Correct. Keep only text and page; throw away the rest.
Runner-up. A summary at the top with headings (key summary + section headers) helps keep a few facts. It cannot hold dozens of rows per page.
Asking for more care does not change how a long input is read.
Correct. A few pages per pass means no page is buried in the middle.

deep.premise: It is easy to treat this as one problem. It is two: the tool sends far more than is used, and the middle of a long input is read less reliably than its ends. The guide's mitigation of a summary at the top with headings helps when a few facts must survive, not when dozens of rows per page must.

questions.question: An MCP tool, get_attachments, returns an empty array both when an invoice genuinely has no attachments and when the attachment store cannot be reached. The store goes offline for 20 to 40 minutes during its nightly index rebuild, which overlaps the extraction run. Last quarter 1.2% of invoices posted as having no supporting documents although a customs declaration existed, and clearance was delayed each time. What is the right fix?

options.t: Retry the store inside the tool with exponential backoff for up to sixty seconds before returning the empty array.
options.why: Runner-up. Local retry of transient failures is good practice and would win if outages lasted seconds. These last 20 to 40 minutes, so after sixty seconds the tool still returns an empty array that looks like 'none'.

options.t: Hold every invoice whose attachment list comes back empty in a review queue until a clerk confirms the documents.
options.why: Incorrect. Most empty results are genuine, so this queues the common case to catch a rare failure, while the tool still hides which is which.

options.t: Compare attachment counts with the ERP after posting, and raise an exception when the two counts disagree.
options.why: Incorrect. It finds the problem after posting, when the clearance delay has already started, and the ERP only knows what extraction gave it.

options.t: Return isError with a transient category and isRetryable: true when unreachable, keeping [] for none found.
options.why: Correct. An outage and a genuine 'no attachments' are opposite facts that share one return value. Separating them lets the agent hold or retry the outage case and proceed on the genuine one.

questions.decider: Outages last 20 to 40 minutes, longer than any local retry, so the tool must report the failure as a failure; if outages lasted seconds, retrying inside the tool would hide them safely.
questions.explanation: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results. Return structured errors (isError, category, retryability) so the agent can choose the right recovery; a shared empty value makes that impossible.

eli5.question: The tool says 'no attachments' both when there are none and when it could not check. The clue is: the store is offline for 20 to 40 minutes at a time. So a quick retry inside the tool will not get past the outage.
eli5.answer: Imagine a receptionist who says 'no messages' both when there are none and when the message system is down. You would never chase anything. They should say 'the system is down, try later' when it is (a structured error with isError). Then 'no messages' means what it says. Rule: 'I couldn't check' must look different from 'there's nothing'.
options: Runner-up. Retrying for a minute (local retry with backoff) would win if outages were short. These last up to 40 minutes.
Holding every empty result sends mostly genuine cases to clerks.
Checking after posting is too late; the delay has already happened.
Correct. 'Couldn't reach the store, try again' versus 'genuinely none'.

deep.premise: Outages are transient, and the textbook answer for transient failures is retry locally. That is right only if the outage ends before the retry gives up. Here outages last 20 to 40 minutes, so the tool must say 'I could not check' instead of 'none'.

questions.question: One prompt classifies each document, extracts its fields, converts amounts to USD and checks business rules, all in a single call. Accuracy dropped when the rule checks were added. When a packing list is read as an invoice, everything downstream is wrong in ways that still pass the rule checks. Whatever its type, every document goes through those four steps in that order, each using the previous step's result. What is the best restructuring?

options.t: Give a coordinator agent the four jobs as tools, and let it choose the next step based on what each result reveals.
options.why: Runner-up. Dynamic decomposition is right when the next step depends on what is found, and would win if documents needed different steps. Here every document takes the same four steps, so a coordinator adds cost and variability for no gain.

options.t: Keep one call, and add an independent reviewer instance that checks the full output before anything is posted.
options.why: Incorrect. Independent review helps catch subtle errors, but a misclassified document can look consistent, and the single call still does four jobs at once.

options.t: Split the work into four sequential calls, with the type from the first call choosing the extraction schema for the next.
options.why: Correct. A fixed sequence of dependent steps is what prompt chaining is for. Each call has one job, and the classification becomes an output that can be checked before extraction relies on it.

options.t: Keep one call, and reorganise the prompt into four headed sections with the classification instructions placed first.
options.why: Incorrect. Headings make a prompt easier to read but leave four jobs competing in one pass, with no checkpoint after classification.

questions.decider: Every document runs the same four steps in the same order, so a fixed chain fits; if the steps varied with what each document revealed, an adaptive coordinator would be better.
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining suits a fixed sequence of dependent steps: each step does one job, and each intermediate result can be checked. Adaptive decomposition is for work whose next step depends on what is found.

eli5.question: One prompt does four jobs at once, and a wrong first guess spoils everything after it. The clue is: every document goes through the same four steps in the same order. So the question is whether you need a fixed assembly line or a manager deciding as you go.
eli5.answer: Think of an assembly line versus a foreman who decides each next step. When every product goes through the same stations in the same order, an assembly line (prompt chaining) is simpler and you can inspect the product between stations. A foreman (adaptive coordinator) helps only when products need different steps. Rule: fixed steps in a fixed order, use a chain.
options: Runner-up. A foreman deciding steps (dynamic decomposition) would win if documents needed different steps.
An inspector at the end (independent review) can be fooled by output that is wrong but consistent.
Correct. Four stations in a row, each checkable before the next.
Headings tidy the prompt; it is still one crowded pass.

deep.premise: 'Agentic' can sound more advanced than a fixed pipeline, so a coordinator choosing steps is tempting. But that flexibility only pays when the steps vary by case. Here they never do: same four steps, same order. A chain is simpler and gives a checkpoint after classification.

questions.question: After extraction, enrichment tools look up the vendor's tax registration and contract terms; they need the vendor identity and document type that extract_metadata establishes. In about 8% of runs the model opens with an enrichment lookup, using a vendor guessed from the filename, and gets another vendor's data. In a further 3% it replies in prose on its first turn without calling any tool. The metadata step has to come first on every request. Which mechanism achieves that?

options.t: Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request, then return to auto.
options.why: Correct. Forcing the named tool makes the first call extract_metadata on every request. It fixes both failures: enrichment cannot go first, and the model cannot answer in prose instead.

options.t: Expand the enrichment tools' descriptions to say vendor identity must come from extract_metadata output.
options.why: Incorrect. Better descriptions improve tool selection but stay probabilistic, and they do nothing for the prose replies.

options.t: Add a pre-call hook that rejects enrichment calls until extract_metadata has returned, with an error naming it.
options.why: Runner-up. A prerequisite gate is the right tool when a call must be blocked until another has run, and would win if wrong ordering were the only failure. It cannot make the model call any tool, so the 3% prose replies still skip the metadata step.

options.t: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} on the first request, and keep it there until metadata exists.
options.why: Incorrect. "any" stops the prose replies but lets the model pick any tool, including an enrichment lookup.

questions.decider: Some runs call no tool at all on the first turn, which a blocking hook cannot fix; if the only failure were enrichment going first, a prerequisite gate would serve as well.
questions.explanation: tool_choice answers different questions: auto lets the model decide, any requires some tool, and a forced named tool requires that specific one. Use the forced setting when a particular tool must run first.

eli5.question: The model sometimes skips the first required step, in two ways. The clue is: in 3% of runs it does not call any tool at all; it just writes an answer. So the fix has to make it call the right tool, not only stop it calling the wrong one.
eli5.answer: Think of a security desk. A guard who stops people going upstairs without a badge (a hook) prevents the wrong order. But someone who walks out without visiting the desk at all is not stopped. Telling the visitor 'your first stop is the badge desk' (forced tool_choice) covers both. Rule: if one specific tool must run first, force that tool.
options: Correct. Forcing the named tool means the first call is always the metadata step.
Better labels (tool descriptions) help, but cannot guarantee anything.
Runner-up. A blocking guard (prerequisite hook) stops enrichment going first. It would win if that were the only problem.
'Must call some tool' (any) still lets it choose the wrong one.

deep.premise: The 8% wrong-order case is the vivid one, and a prerequisite hook is the textbook fix for wrong order. But a hook only reacts to calls the model makes. In the 3% prose case the model makes no call, so nothing is blocked and metadata never runs. Forcing the named tool covers both failures.
